position: The economy is growing above its own recent average with modest capacity tightness, and the expansion is led by investment and the production chain rather than by the consumer. Inflation has risen for nine consecutive months on every measure computed here and policy has turned tighter. Net corporate profitability is being held up by an unusually low interest burden at the moment that support is being withdrawn. Meanwhile the market has fallen while the economy grew — a valuation event rather than an activity event — which is why so many sectors screen cheap against their own history at once.

components.note: Component contributions to the headline are not reported for this quarter: the statistical residual is 29.1% of the attributed total, the largest in the series. Each component's own growth rate is published and valid.

industry.note: Capital goods and intermediates supply 53% of industrial growth on 30% of the weight. Everyday consumer goods supply 4% on 16%.

slack.note: The z-score excludes the current reading from its own benchmark. Inventories are normal; the order book cannot be read because the survey panel grew from 385 to 432 companies while the aggregate rose 9.3%.

corporate.note: Operating profitability is below its recent normal while net profitability is at normal. The difference is debt service, and the interest burden sits 1.41 standard deviations below normal. Net margins are held up by cheap debt rather than by operating performance, at the moment policy has turned.

inflation.note: India publishes no core inflation series; every core figure in circulation is derived by whoever quotes it. We report two constructions from MoSPI's published indices and weights and state both, so agreement or divergence is visible. All three measures have risen for nine consecutive months, so this is not a food story. House rent carries 28% of the non-food basket at 2.74%, which holds the excluding-food measure down.

inflation_sources.note: Food and personal care together supply 62% of all inflation from 42% of the basket. Personal care delivers 2.6 times its weight.

checks.note: Each check sets two separate measurements of the same thing against each other, taken by different institutions using different methods. A disagreement is reported, not averaged away. Consumption carries the sector call: total household spending grows far faster than output of the goods mass-market households buy.

growth.text: Real GDP grew **7.82%** in the latest quarter, **+0.35 percentage points above** its own 13-quarter average of 7.47%. With only 13 readings on this base that average is a run rate, not a measure of normal growth.

industry.text: Industrial growth is led by **investment and the production chain**. Capital goods and intermediates carry 30% of the index and supply **53%** of its growth; consumer categories carry 27% and supply **19%**. The largest single contributor is **Intermediate Goods** at +9.21%. Intermediate goods are the inputs firms buy before they produce, so this is a forward-looking signal pointing up.

Consumption is **narrow**. Durable goods output grew +7.97% against +1.77% for everyday goods — a gap of **6.20 points**. Spending is concentrated in higher-income households, or in services the production index does not measure. Either reading points allocation away from consumer staples.

inflation.text: Headline inflation is **5.54%**, having risen in **every one of the last 8 months**. Excluding food it is 4.48%, and the typical division of the basket is at 5.01%. Across the series the excluding-food measure has moved +1.39 points and the typical division +2.89 points, which makes this **broad-based**. Were this a food shock, the excluding-food measure would be flat.

policy.text: The policy rate was moved to **5.50%** on 9 October 2026. With headline inflation at 5.54% against a 4.0% target midpoint, and rising on every measure, the direction of policy is **tightening**, not neutral.

corporate.text: Operating profitability sits **below** its recent normal at -0.41 standard deviations, while net profitability sits **at** normal at +0.13. The difference between them is debt service, and the interest burden is **-1.41 standard deviations below** normal. **Net margins are held up by unusually cheap debt rather than by operating performance** — and policy is tightening into exactly that support. Interest coverage at 6.09 against a median of 5.40, with 1 of 50 industry groups unable to cover interest, makes this a margin question and not a solvency one.

slack.text: Capacity utilisation is **76.30%** against a trailing median of 74.65% — a gap of +1.65 points and **+0.80 standard deviations** against the preceding window. That is **modestly tight**, not an extreme.

Inventories relative to sales are **normal** — 66.12% against a trailing median of 65.63%, +0.07 standard deviations. Any reading of an inventory build-up here would be an artefact of measuring against a long-run average rather than a recent one.

The order book cannot be read. The published figure is an average per responding company and the survey panel grew **12.2%**, from 385 to 432 firms. The per-company average is **-2.56%** while the derived aggregate is **+9.33%**. A growing panel drags a per-company average down with no change in demand, so the two cannot be separated and **no conclusion rests on this series**.

market.text: **The market has fallen while the economy grew.** The benchmark returned **-12.33%** over twelve months to 2026-10-27 against real GDP growth of 7.82%. A decline of that size alongside growth of that size is a **valuation event, not an activity event** — prices fell against earnings that did not. That is the context for every valuation reading below, and it is why so many sectors screen cheap against their own history at the same time.

Price is common to both ratios, so reading them together separates two different kinds of cheap. Across 21 indices: **2** are cheap against earnings **and** book (Bankex, LowVol) — price is simply low. **7** are cheap on earnings while expensive on book (Financials, Healthcare, Auto, Teck, DivFocus, Industrials and 1 others) — return on book is historically high, so the cheapness rests on **elevated earnings** rather than a low price, and it lasts only as long as those earnings do. **3** are paid for on both (Power, Quality, ConsDiscr). Only **Bankex** combine cheapness on both measures with outperformance.

factors.text:
Factor returns against the benchmark:
- **Value**: -3.05% over twelve months (+9.28 against the benchmark), PE 8.76, PE percentile 51
- **DivStability**: -4.09% over twelve months (+8.25 against the benchmark), PE 11.49, PE percentile 30
- **Quality**: -8.42% over twelve months (+3.92 against the benchmark), PE 27.06, PE percentile 67
- **DivFocus**: -8.76% over twelve months (+3.58 against the benchmark), PE 21.27, PE percentile 12
- **Momentum**: -11.92% over twelve months (+0.42 against the benchmark), PE 23.30, PE percentile 54
- **LowVol**: -14.33% over twelve months (-1.99 against the benchmark), PE 24.41, PE percentile 10

**DivStability** is the best combination in the set — it has outperformed by +8.25 points and still sits at the 30th percentile of its own valuation history. With policy tightening into companies whose net margins lean on cheap debt service, the firms able to pay dividends are the firms that do not need the debt.

**LowVol** is cheap at the 10th percentile and has underperformed by -1.99 points. Cheap and not working needs a catalyst that cannot be named from this data.

coverage.text: This analysis runs on the data available at the time of generation. market indices excluded as stale: BSE100, BSE200, BSE500, FMCG, IT, MidCap, SmallCap; figures using a stored value rather than a live one: cu, inv, ord. Figures drawn from a stored value remain correct as published but do not reflect releases since.

confidence.text: Of 8 independent cross-checks — each setting two separate measurements of the same thing against each other — **5 agree**, **1 disagree**, **1 cannot be read** and **1 could not be run**. A disagreement is reported, not averaged away: where two methods differ, the difference is the finding.

reconciliation.text: **The two are not competing forecasts and are not averaged.** The regime model ranks sectors on realised volatility, because its own validation found volatility ranking stable across folds while return ranking was not. It therefore sets **total exposure** and breaks ties. The fundamental engine ranks on macro direction and valuation against each sector's own history, and sets **direction**. Where they differ, it means low volatility has met a weak fundamental case — not that two return forecasts disagree.

Across 15 sectors the two models take a position on the same name **5** times. They **agree 4** times — Auto, Telecom, Realty, Power and **conflict 1** time — ConsDiscr. On the remaining 10 only one model has a view, so there is nothing to reconcile. The conflict resolves to **neutral**: a sector can be calm and still be expensive, and low volatility is not a reason to pay a high multiple. Where a theme has a cheaper expression, the exposure goes there instead.

Total equity exposure is **100%**, set by the regime model rather than by the macro view. If the crisis state is confirmed for five consecutive days, exposure falls to 25% and the whole book scales with it. **That is a stop, not a forecast** — and the honest caveat travels with it: the crisis overlay rests on a single episode, so its drawdown protection is one observation rather than a repeated result.

The factor sleeve is where the volatility ranking misleads most. The regime model's largest factor overweight is the least volatile factor — true by construction, and silent on return. On the evidence, **Value** leads at +9.28 points against the benchmark and **LowVol** trails at -1.99 points. Following the volatility ladder would overweight the laggard and underweight the leader. Use the quant sleeve to size risk; use the fundamental ranking to choose factors.

market_table.note: Sorted by PE percentile, cheapest against its own five-year history first. Price is common to both ratios, so reading them together separates a low price from merely elevated earnings.

factor_table.note: Ranked by return against the benchmark. The regime model ranks these on volatility instead, which is why the two sleeves differ.

reco_agreement.note: Regime Normal, equity exposure 100%. The regime model ranks on realised volatility, not expected return, so a conflict means low volatility has met a weak fundamental case — not that two return forecasts disagree.

reco_book.note: The macro sets direction, the regime model sets total exposure and breaks ties. If the crisis state is confirmed for five consecutive days, exposure falls to 25% and the whole book scales with it. That is a stop, not a forecast.
